transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Anika Rao (CTO - Summit), Jamal Ortiz (SRE Lead), Priya Singh (ML Platform)

Summary:
Short technical deep dive focused on p95/p99 tail behavior observed by Summit Telemetrics in production. Main themes: multi-hop network amplification, KV-cache hotkey behavior, streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs for tail latency, and quantization/batching implications in a VPC/on-prem topology. Action items and a plan for a 24h tail capture and an on-prem pilot were agreed.

Topics:
- Observed tail spikes and correlation with specific inter-AZ hops
- Streaming fallback strategies when latency SLOs are threatened
- KV cache hotkey mitigation and sharding considerations
- Batching windows, continuous batching, and quantization impacts on p95/p99
- On-prem/VPC peering constraints and NIC RX/TX behavior

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, quick roll call?
[00:05] Anika Rao: Anika here. Hey Maya, hi Daniel.
[00:07] Jamal Ortiz: Jamal on the call.
[00:09] Priya Singh: Priya, good afternoon.
[00:11] Daniel Park: Daniel from Redwood, thanks for making time.
[00:14] Maya Chen: Cool, objective for today: dig into the p95/p99 tail notes you sent over, validate root causes and propose mitigations we can try in a 2-week on-prem pilot. Sound right?
[00:20] Anika Rao: Yup that's right. We're seeing occasional p99 jumps from ~180ms to 1.2s with no CPU/GPU spikes, so it looks like something network-y or cache-y.
[00:28] Daniel Park: OK, that pattern often means network amplification or KV cache hot shard. Can you remind us of the topology? VPC peering, transit, cross-AZ?
[00:34] Jamal Ortiz: Sure, high-level: app tier in AZ-a talks to Redwood private endpoints through a transit VPC, we have cross-AZ peering for failover. Most inference traffic is regional but we do have occasional cross-region fallbacks to the backup region.
[00:46] Priya Singh: Also worth noting: we use a mix of streaming for interactive chat and non-streaming for longer prompt completions. Streaming is default for user-facing chat.
[00:55] Maya Chen: Good. On the p99 jump — do you see it correlate to a particular flow (streaming vs non-streaming) or specific model size?
[01:02] Anika Rao: It seems worse for interactive streaming — token-by-token responses. Non-streaming comps usually sit at a tighter tail. But streaming has more variance.
[01:10] Daniel Park: That's consistent. Streaming keeps the request open and is more sensitive to head-of-line delays on the path. If a network hop transiently delays a packet the rest of the streaming tokens get delayed and it shows as tail amplification.
[01:22] Jamal Ortiz: We also saw the spikes happen when we had a KV cache miss ratio increase — like when a hot key warms or dies; thought that might be unrelated.
[01:30] Daniel Park: Not unrelated. If you get a KV miss the runtime does additional work (KV fetches from backing store) which can add tens to hundreds ms depending on where the backing store sits. Combine that with an intermittent cross-AZ hop and you've got p99 outliers.
[01:42] Priya Singh: We're on a mixed setup—some models quantized to 8-bit, some 4-bit experimental. Does quantization amplify the tail? We thought quantization should reduce latency.
[01:50] Daniel Park: Quantization generally reduces compute latency but can change runtime memory patterns — e.g., for KV cache sizes and alignment. In practice quantization reduces average token latency but doesn't fix network-induced tails. Sometimes a quantized path increases kernel prefetch variability on GPUs — rare, but seen on older drivers.
[02:06] Maya Chen: Let's annotate likely contributors: network hops, KV miss + backing store latency, hot-shard keys, streaming sensitivity. Any others?
[02:14] Jamal Ortiz: Autoscaling cold starts? We run Dedicated reserved pools so cold-starts are rare, but when autoscaling happens in the serving tier there's brief variance.
[02:22] Daniel Park: Right — and batching behavior matters. Are you using continuous batching or fixed-window batching?
[02:27] Priya Singh: We use a small continuous batcher configured by Redwood's defaults, target latency 80ms and batch cap 32.
[02:34] Daniel Park: Continuous batching helps throughput, but in streaming we often flush smaller batches for token streaming; it can produce more HEAD-OF-LINE because small batches increase variability. For tail mitigation we can favor smaller batch caps for streams or separate pools with different batching/kind.
[02:48] Anika Rao: We also saw p99 spikes tied to a particular host once, suspected a NIC interrupt storm during a noisy neighbor moment. Could be cloud infra issue too.
[02:58] Daniel Park: Yep, NIC saturation or driver-level IRQ smoothing can cause sub-ms to 100s ms bursts depending on queueing. On-prem can be worse if NIC buffers are small or jumbo frames mismatched.
[03:10] Maya Chen: Proposed short-term mitigations: 1) separate streaming pool with strict batch cap and pre-warmed concurrency, 2) KV hotkey sharding + local L1 cache to cut backing-store trips, 3) network route pinning to avoid cross-AZ fallback during spikes, 4) streaming fallback to non-streaming when tail exceeds threshold. Thoughts?
[03:28] Jamal Ortiz: The streaming fallback idea — tell me more. Do you mean converting streaming requests to non-streaming if we detect a hop increase?
[03:33] Daniel Park: Exactly. You can implement a fallback policy: attempt streaming, if token latency for the first N tokens exceeds a threshold for Xms, fall back to non-streaming completion for that request. It reduces perceived tail for the end user at the cost of losing incremental tokens. For most UIs that's acceptable if the full response arrives quicker than continued streaming would.
[03:48] Priya Singh: User experience concerns though — some users expect streaming immediacy. Maybe fallback only after we hit p95-based triggers and only for non-interactive users.
[03:56] Maya Chen: Right — we can make it conditional: fallback policy per route with TTL. Redwood Console supports route-level policies and automatic fallback to a compatible model variant.
[04:05] Anika Rao: On the KV side, we have a Redis cluster in the Transit VPC that sometimes gets flushy. Would a local L1 inside the inference plane help?
[04:13] Daniel Park: Yes. Redwood's runtime supports a small local L1 prefix/KV cache in-memory that handles hot keys for a short TTL. We can tune eviction and fingerprinting to avoid staleness. That kills a lot of miss-induced p99s. Sharding hot keys across shards or consistent-hashing them to avoid hotspot is also effective.
[04:28] Jamal Ortiz: Do you have a recommended approach for sharding? We currently use a single Redis shard per region for simplicity.
[04:34] Daniel Park: Two recommendations: 1) add a small hash-based shard ring for hot keys (route-based) and route cache writes to that ring; 2) use client-side key prefixing by route to distribute. We can provide an RFC config for this.
[04:46] Priya Singh: About measuring — we'll need high-fidelity p95/p99 breakdowns by route and by network hop. How do you capture packet-level hop mapping?
[04:55] Maya Chen: Redwood's tracing hooks can annotate requests with network path metadata and export trace spans by hop; for private deployments we can also capture tail-snapshots (first-byte and last-byte timestamps) and stitch with VPC flow logs. We'll run a 24h tail capture to correlate spikes.
[05:08] Anika Rao: Sounds good. Any quick wins we can do now without infra changes?
[05:12] Daniel Park: Short wins: reduce streaming batch caps, enable local L1 cache for hot routes, tune KV timeouts to fail-fast (so the runtime can fallback instead of blocking), and set streaming fallback thresholds. Those are config-only.
[05:24] Jamal Ortiz: What about quantization and batching interplay — if we move more models to 4-bit, do we risk increasing p99 due to alignment and kernel jitter?
[05:32] Daniel Park: In our experience 4-bit improves throughput and average latency but you must watch memory alignment and kernel selection. On some GPUs, certain quant kernels endure slight variance under memory pressure; we saw this with older cuBLAS versions. We'll recommend specific kernel profiles and driver versions in the bench doc.
[05:46] Priya Singh: For the on-prem pilot, what hardware should we provision? We have racks with A10s and some H100s on order.
[05:53] Daniel Park: H100s are ideal for throughput but for interactive streaming the A10 can be more predictable depending on batch sizes. For tail testing it's good to have both and run A/B: A10 for the streaming pool, H100 for the batch non-streaming pool. Also collect NIC metrics and interrupt rates.
[06:06] Anika Rao: Ok that aligns with hardware planning.
[06:09] Maya Chen: Let's walk through a proposed 2-week plan: week 1 - config changes in hosted/dedicated to apply local L1 cache, smaller streaming batch caps, enable early-fail KV timeouts, run 24h tail capture; week 2 - on-prem pilot with A10/H100 and latency microbench plus simulated hotkey storms. Any red flags?
[06:25] Jamal Ortiz: No red flags. We need to ensure firewall rules and VPC peering are ready for the pilot.
[06:30] Daniel Park: We'll prepare scripts to replay your traffic profile and a synthetic hotkey injector to simulate cache storms. We'll also include a streaming->non-streaming fallback harness.
[06:39] Priya Singh: One more question: does Redwood's runtime expose per-token timing so we can see where the delay is (serialization vs network vs kernel)?
[06:46] Daniel Park: Yes — per-token timing is available through tracing hooks. We can annotate token serialization, KV lookup, kernel execution, and outbound wire time. That will let us pinpoint whether it's network or compute.
[06:57] Anika Rao: Good — that will be essential.
[07:00] Maya Chen: Going back to route-level policies — we'll suggest a canary: route A with strict streaming caps and L1 on, route B baseline. Compare p95/p99. We'll also recommend a short-term network pinning policy to avoid long cross-AZ fallbacks during the window.
[07:15] Jamal Ortiz: How invasive is pinning? It sounds risky for failover.
[07:18] Daniel Park: It can be conservative: we pin for 30s after a route-level threshold and allow normal failover otherwise. It's a tradeoff between availability and consistent latency; we'll include options.
[07:28] Priya Singh: Any compliance/security issues for collecting the 24h trace? We need to mask PII before sharing.
[07:34] Maya Chen: Absolutely. For hosted we'd use redaction hooks; for private we'll run the capture locally and share redacted metrics. We'll follow your compliance checklist and can sign an NDA addendum if needed.
[07:44] Anika Rao: Great.
[07:46] (short silence)
[07:48] Maya Chen: OK let's recap next steps.
[07:50] Maya Chen: Redwood will: 1) share a benchmark spreadsheet and recommended kernel/driver versions, 2) run a 24h tail capture config on a staging route and share p95/p99 CSV, 3) provide the hotkey injector and replay scripts for your pilot.
[08:03] Anika Rao: Summit will: 1) provide traffic profile and VPC peering docs, 2) stand up pilot hosts (A10/H100) and open access, 3) share 72h traces.
[08:14] Jamal Ortiz: We'll also check NIC stats and provide any cloud provider incident logs if present.
[08:19] Priya Singh: I'll coordinate with infra and schedule the on-prem windows.
[08:22] Daniel Park: I'll draft the microbench harness and upload to the shared drive, link in the follow-up email.
[08:28] Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up with timestamps and the spreadsheet.
[08:30] Anika Rao: Thanks. Bye.

End of transcript.
